title: What Was Put in Front
aliases: The Height of a Bowed Head
logline: A white church stands two hundred metres from the surf on a strip of sand with a lagoon behind it, and nearly every account of how it began has the same three things in it, a tree, an image and money, in a different order; the earliest printed mention of its altar that research has reached is a colonial footnote about a knot of young leaves that did two jobs at once. The text being taught says the same act is sorted only by what is put in front of it, and the film, shot at noon on the day the sun stands straight overhead, is about how little of that a picture can hold.
human_question: When one act can be done for two reasons at once, who is in a position to say which one it was done for?

place.what_kind_of_place: A Catholic pilgrimage church of the nineteenth century, large and white, on a low peninsula of sand between the open sea and a wide, shallow lagoon, the strip about three kilometres across at this point. The sea is a couple of hundred metres from the church's west side; the lagoon's still water lies to the east beyond coconut and palmyra gardens and scrub. In front of the church is an old banyan that the shrine's own tradition connects with its beginning. Around it lies a very large open ground of sand, built for the two annual feasts, when hundreds of thousands of people camp here; on most days of the year it is almost empty.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: With the sound off it is a film about light and an exact geometry. For a few minutes on two days a year the sun stands directly over this latitude at noon and upright things lose their shadows: the palms stand on dark discs of their own crowns, the church's white front has no shadow in any recess, the banyan's shade lies exactly under it. From the air the place is a clean diagram: surf, a pale strip, a white building, palms, and a second, flat, glassy water. The film is built around that noon, with a locked drone looking straight down, and it resolves on its own terms when the drone rises vertically out of the one shape of a tree and its shade until both waters are in the frame.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing moves, deliberately. The surf on the west side, the wind in the palm fronds, heat shimmer over the empty sand ground, crows. The only change the film is built on is the sun's: in the late morning the palms throw short shadows to the south or north, and at noon on the zenith day they throw none. The camera is locked for every shot but the last, which is a single vertical rise.
place.when_it_looks_best: Clear sky at solar noon (about 12:10 local time at this longitude) on or within a day of the two dates when the sun passes directly overhead at this latitude, computed at about 11 April and about 2 September. Both dates fall outside the two feasts (the March feast and the main feast at the end of July), so the ground is empty. The April date has the calmer sea; the September date follows the south-west monsoon winds and may be hazier.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: The noon film. A church by the sea on a pale strip of sand, filmed in the one light that most films avoid: sun straight overhead, no modelling, no long shadows, white on white. Locked frames of palms, a banyan, a white façade and an empty feast ground; a locked drone looking straight down at a tree whose shade is exactly underneath it; then one slow vertical rise until the sea is on one side of the frame and the lagoon on the other. It holds as a piece of pure design and heat, with surf for its only music.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The voice sets three tellings of the church's beginning side by side without choosing among them: a traveller who commits himself to the saint and builds a chapel as his business prospers; a trader who promises a church if his business recovers; a saint who supplies the gold for the building. The same tree, image and money occur in each, in a different order; a fourth, later telling has no money in it at all. The text being taught sorts the ordinary acts of earning, keeping and spending by exactly that, by what is placed in front of them: earning and the like, done with faith, kindness or compassion foremost, raise no unwholesome mind, nor do earning, guarding and spending with wisdom foremost for their use; and earning and guarding wealth are on its list of the everyday occasions of wanting. Then the document: a colonial secretary's footnote of 1850 describing trees bound with a band of young leaves, dedicated to spirits, gods, a Buddhist temple and, he says, this altar; in his own words the band marked the fruit as an offering and, it was presumed, kept thieves off the garden until it was ripe. One knot, an offering and a guard. He wrote that there was 'reason to fear' the owners gave little and kept the rest, of the offerings made to spirits. The text's factor of decision settles on an object and holds it, true or false, and the film does not say which way any reading of that fruit went. The overhead sun is the film's answer: the most complete light of the day shows the surface of everything and nothing of what it was for.

sequence.on_screen: Late morning. Drone high and oblique from over the surf, looking inland: breakers, a pale strip of sand about three kilometres wide, a white church among palms close to the beach, and beyond the gardens the flat, glassy sheet of the lagoon. Locked, held for a long time.
sequence.voice: A church on a strip of sand between the sea and a lagoon. Nearly every account of how it began has three things in it: a tree, an image of Saint Anne, and money. The accounts do not agree about the order they came in, and one of them has no money in it at all.

sequence.on_screen: Ground, 35 mm on a tripod: the banyan in front of the church, its hanging roots and deep shade; the empty sand ground behind it, heat shimmer, a crow walking. No people.
sequence.voice: In one telling, which the missionaries who later ran the shrine give as tradition, a tired traveller commends himself to the saint, sleeps under a tree, dreams of her image, wakes and finds it, puts a shelter over it, and builds a chapel as his business prospers. In a telling printed much later, a trader wrecked on this coast promises to build a church if his business recovers. In another, the saint herself gives him the gold to build it.

sequence.on_screen: The church front, wide and square-on, locked, in near-overhead light: white on white, almost no shadow in the doorways or under the cornices.
sequence.voice: The text taught in this series sorts the same act by what is put in front of it. Earning wealth and the like, done with faith or kindness or compassion placed foremost, raise no unwholesome mind; nor do earning, keeping and spending it with wisdom placed foremost, for their use. Earning and guarding wealth are also on its list of the ordinary occasions when wanting mostly arises. The three tellings put the faith and the prosperity in different places. The building is the same in all of them.

sequence.on_screen: Coconut palms in a garden near the church, long lens, trunks in rows, the fronds moving; nothing tied to any of them.
sequence.voice: In 1850 James Emerson Tennent, who had been the colony's colonial secretary, published a book on the progress of Christianity on the island. In a footnote he describes fruit trees along a road far to the south with a band of young leaves fastened round the trunk: a tree devoted to a spirit, or to a god, sometimes to a Buddhist temple, and even, he writes, to the altar of Saint Anne on this coast. The trees he saw were not these. The altar he names is, as far as the record shows, this one.

sequence.on_screen: A single palm trunk, close, from its base upward, the ringed bark in hard vertical light; the camera does not move.
sequence.voice: In his own words the band did two things. It marked the fruit as promised, to be picked when ripe and sent as an offering. And while it hung there, it was presumed, no thief would venture into the garden. One knot: an offering and a guard. The text has a place for each, faith placed foremost on one side, guarding what one has on the other, and it names taking what is not given as a harm done through wanting. It gives no way of telling the two aims apart by looking at the knot.

sequence.on_screen: The empty feast ground at noon from a low tripod: sand, a line of shelters, shimmer, the church small at the edge of frame.
sequence.voice: Tennent added that there was, in his words, reason to fear the spirits were to some extent defrauded of their due: that the custom was to offer a few of the finest fruit and keep the rest. He wrote it of the offerings made to spirits, not of this altar. The text describes a factor it calls decision, which settles on an object and holds it without asking whether it is true or false, and says it very often holds the false as true. It gives no way to tell, from a page, what any owner put in front of his fruit. Neither can this film.

sequence.on_screen: Solar noon on the zenith day. The drone directly above the banyan, looking straight down, locked: crown and shade are one dark shape on the sand. Held for twenty seconds. Then a single vertical rise, no tilt, until the church roof, the surf on one side and the lagoon on the other are all in the frame.
sequence.voice: Under every telling there is one more thing: the wish to do something, to build. The text says that wish is not the force that makes a mind stick; beside wanting it feeds wanting, and beside a good mind it works against it. On this day the sun stands straight over the tree and its shade has nowhere to fall but underneath. From here the whole of it is visible, and none of what it was for.

concept_merge.why_together: C005 carries the film because its test is the one every account of this church already raises. The Margaya lists earning wealth, acquiring it and guarding what has been acquired among the ordinary occasions on which greed-rooted minds mostly arise [C005-M:L5], then exempts earning and the like when faith, loving-kindness or compassion is placed foremost, and earning, guarding and spending when wisdom is placed foremost with regard to usefulness [C005-M:L9]; its verb is placing in front (පෙරදැරි කර ගෙන). The shrine's tellings differ exactly on what is in front: faith first and prosperity after, prosperity as the condition of the building, or wealth given for the building (and one later telling has no vow and no money). The 1850 footnote supplies a single documented act that holds both aims at once, an offering and a guard against theft, and theft is one of the courses of action the text says are done with greed-rooted minds [C005-M:L3]. C021 supplies the two factors the story actually turns on. The wish-to-do behind a vow or a building is not greed: it is the wish to take up the object, not the force that sticks [C021-P:L69], and it follows the mind it joins, feeding greed in a greed-rooted mind and helping to suppress it in a wholesome one [C021-P:L75] [C021-M:L27]. And the text's account of any settled verdict is the decision factor, which fixes on its object without separating true from false and often holds the false as true [C021-P:L45]; the film sets it beside the footnote's suspicion as a caution about readings in general, never as a report of what was in its author's mind.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the question the text asks cannot be answered from where a camera stands, or from where a colonial secretary stood. C005 alone would make this a film about motives at a shrine, and would put the pilgrims under a lens the text does not give anyone. C021 turns the lens round: in the text, settling on a reading of someone else's aim is the work of a mental factor with no colour of its own [C021-P:L25], and the wish that built the church is the same kind of wish whichever way it faced. Together they let the film say what the text says, that the aim is the whole difference, and show what the text implies, that the aim is not in the picture.

concept_links.why: The Margaya says seven of the ten unwholesome courses of action, taking what is not given among them, are done with greed-rooted minds [C005-M:L3]; lists earning wealth, acquiring it, guarding what has been acquired and giving wealth to obtain dear things among the occasions when greed-rooted minds mostly arise [C005-M:L5]; and exempts the same acts when faith, loving-kindness or compassion is placed foremost, or wisdom with regard to usefulness [C005-M:L9]. This church's record asks that question twice, not by analogy: its founding tellings differ precisely on whether faith or prosperity came first (one later telling has neither vow nor money), and the oldest printed mention of its altar is a footnote describing a dedicated tree whose band of leaves was both an offering and a guard against theft. Exemption ruling, read from the source line: undecidable, by design, on every count. The tellings cannot be ruled because they disagree on the very order the text makes decisive; the band on the tree carries both aims in one act; and the vows and offerings of pilgrims, then and now, are never examined, because the text gives an observer no access to what another placed foremost. The film never calls any of these acts wholesome: M:L9 says only that no unwholesome mind arises, and the digest records that only feeding animals as a kindness is called wholesome outright [C005-M:L21]. does_not_transfer lines that bind the film: 'Only intentions matter' — the text still names theft as a harm through wanting, so the voice says so and does not dissolve the guard against thieves into motive; 'Minimalism or self-denial is virtue' — the church's size and richness are shown as simply what they are, and the text's own allowance for wealth earned and spent with faith or wisdom foremost is stated; 'Attachment to family is toxic' and 'Art and sport are sinful' do not arise, and the 1806 hymn quoted in the research is not treated as enjoyment.

The six occasional factors occur in wholesome and unwholesome minds alike and take the moral quality of the mind they join [C021-P:L25]. Two of them carry the story. Desire-to-act, the wish to build behind every telling of this church, is the wish to take up the object and not a force that makes it stick [C021-P:L69]; in greed-rooted minds it supports greed, in wholesome minds it helps suppress it [C021-P:L75] [C021-M:L27]. Decision settles firmly on its object without distinguishing true from false or good from bad, and very often holds the false as true [C021-P:L45]; the Margaya adds that it is hard to discern [C021-M:L15]. The 1850 footnote's suspicion about other people's offerings (itself hedged: 'there is reason to fear') is not attributed a mental factor: the film sets the text's account of decision beside it as a caution about readings in general, says neither that the suspicion was wrong nor that it was right, and does not narrate its author's mind. does_not_transfer lines that bind the film: 'Trust your gut, if you're sure it's right' is the line the Tennent beat is built against; 'Hard work is always virtuous' — the effort that built the church is not praised as a virtue; 'Desire is the enemy' — the wish to build is explicitly said to be able to work against wanting; the air-element account of rapture is not used, and nobody's gladness at the shrine is described.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That in these texts the same act, a building, a gift, a knot of leaves round a tree, can come from quite different aims, and that the aim, not the act, is what the texts sort; that the wish to do something is not itself wanting and can run either way; and that a firm reading of someone else's aim, however confident, is a mental event of the reader's and not a fact about the person read. The proof on screen needs no belief: a tree and its shade seen from straight above at noon are one shape, and nothing in that shape says what anything was for.
what_must_be_real: The zenith noon, on the computed date and filmed on it, not simulated with a high-noon frame on another day; if the day is clouded, the payoff is not faked and the film waits for the second date or the next year. The church, the tree and the empty ground as they are on an ordinary day, with no feast, no service, no pilgrim and no devotional act in frame. No band of leaves is tied to any tree for the film, and none is shown: the practice is described from the 1850 text only, and if a banded tree is seen in a garden it is not filmed, because it is someone's present act of devotion or protection. No image, relic, candle or votive object is filmed in close-up. The quotations from the 1850 footnote are read from the printed text, and the three tellings are voiced as tellings, with the traveller telling attributed only to the Oblate record of tradition, not to Bishop Bonjean, since the source reached ties only the seventeenth-century dating to him.
position_hint: Late in the group, after the films about particular kinds of taking and keeping and after the festival film about dancing done as an offering and watched for enjoyment: this one takes the group's recurring rule, that the same act is sorted by its aim, to the point where it cannot be applied from outside at all, and hands the question back to the viewer. It also sets up C021's claim that wanting-to-do is not the problem, which the group's other effort films develop.
risks: Framing pilgrims or petitioners as wanting. The shrine is a living place of vows; a film about the aims behind offerings can be read as a comment on everyone who makes one. The guard is structural: no pilgrim appears, the film is shot outside both feasts, the voice never mentions present-day vows, and its thesis is that no observer can see what another placed foremost.

Endorsing the 1850 suspicion. Tennent's line that the owners kept most of the fruit is quoted as his, with its own hedge ('there is reason to fear'), is said to concern offerings to spirits and not this altar, and is answered only by the text's account of decision; the voice never says the owners did or did not keep the fruit.

Entering a religious argument. Tennent wrote as a Protestant official about Catholic, Hindu, Buddhist and folk practice together; the film does not rank or compare any tradition, and does not use his word for the practice ('superstition').
Narrating a miracle as fact. The dream, the found image, the gold and the light in the tree are told only as what the tellings say.
Averaging the tellings into one founding story, or presenting the 1999 or later versions as older than they can be shown to be.
Letting 'undecidable' turn into 'probably greed'. The voice gives both halves of the text's rule every time it gives one.
Presenting the palms in frame as the trees Tennent saw; he saw his on a road far to the south, and the voice says so.
C006's line about views that justify taking ('the gods gave us these') must not be placed near this film; it would map a wrong view onto a living community's faith.
A shrine on a coast with a nearby military presence: the drone may be refused, and without the overhead shot the payoff does not exist.

Narrating a named person's mind. Tennent's suspicion is quoted as a sentence on a page; the voice never says it was a decision, a misjudgement or a correct one, and never says what he believed. The C021 decision factor is stated as the text's general account only.
drop_if: Drone flight directly over the church ground at noon is refused by the Diocese or the Civil Aviation Authority, and no equivalent overhead position (a mast or tower) is permitted.
The Diocese asks that the film not discuss the origin tellings or the 1850 footnote, or not be made outside a feast.
The banyan in front of the church no longer stands or cannot be filmed without people under it, and no other old tree on the ground carries the payoff.

On inspection the identification of the altar named in the 1850 footnote with this shrine fails (for instance if a separate St Anne's church stood in the peninsula's town in 1850), in which case the footnote leaves the film and the film is too thin without it.

connections.note: The group's throne film holds one surviving object whose every change of hands is on record and whose makeup three visitors with foreign embassies described three ways; it rules the chair's history undecidable under the same two lines of the text (earning, guarding, giving wealth, against the same acts done with usefulness foremost). This film applies that rule to aims no document can record, and swaps that film's night interior, one lamp and macro for noon, open sky and a straight-down drone.

At the time of this audit the IDEA-0018 file still holds a confirmed film about a hill-station town built to deliver another country's sensations; the blind GRP-02 selection proposes rewriting it as a night procession whose dancing is by its own statement an offering, watched from paid seats, with its charge on the seat and the lens. If that rewrite goes ahead: both films are about one act with a devotional aim and a second possible aim; that one puts the second aim in the observer's seat, this one refuses to put it anywhere, because the text gives the observer no way in. Night, handheld and crowd there; noon, locked and empty here.

Another group's film: a Buddhist island shrine where a village builds a coconut-leaf offering pavilion for one day and takes it apart. Coconut leaf as offering there, a band of coconut leaf as offering and guard at once here; a living ritual filmed as it happens there, a practice known only from a printed footnote here, and nobody performing it on camera.

Another group's film on the same peninsula's district: an empty red cape reached by a park track, heat haze, no architecture and no people. Same heat and emptiness, different ground: this film has one large building and its payoff is an overhead geometry, not a horizon.

The group's seafront-lawn film also argues that the same act is wanting or not according to its aim and that the aim does not show, filmed as a whole day on one lawn in fast time. The overlap in argument is real and is stated rather than hidden: that film rests on a stone that states an official purpose and on a crowd whose aims are never read; this one rests on founding tellings that disagree about the order of faith and prosperity and on a footnote in which one knot carries two aims. Cinema is opposite: a crowd in time-lapse there, an empty ground and one locked overhead noon here.

selection.reason: Kept on the blind GRP-02 selection's proposal after testing it, with its story rebuilt: the proposal rested on a 1999 newspaper feature, and research took the shrine's documented record back to 1850 (a colonial secretary's printed footnote naming its altar, and the northern vicariate's report of the same year, reached through the Oblates' historical dictionary), found an Oblate record of tradition in which faith comes first and prosperity after, and found that the footnote itself describes one act with two aims. The shrine's tellings disagree on exactly the order the text makes decisive. Weaknesses stated rather than hidden: the founding tellings are legend; the footnote's trees were elsewhere and only its altar is here; the film's visual strength depends on a single overhead noon shot that needs drone permission over a living shrine.

review.note: This record's body was replaced in full on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-02 re-selection. The previous status was already pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset, but under standing decision 9 any earlier reading of this record no longer applies. The concepts are unchanged (C005 primary, C021 supporting). The location, proposed by Claude, is the Catholic pilgrimage shrine of Saint Anne on the sand peninsula of the north-west coast, which was the blind selection's proposal; it was tested and kept, and the story beneath it rebuilt. The proposal's earliest source was a 1999 newspaper feature; the record now rests on a printed book of 1850 whose footnote names the shrine's altar as one to which trees were dedicated by a band of young leaves that, in the author's words, both marked the fruit as an offering and kept thieves off the garden, and on the Oblate record of tradition, in which a traveller's faith comes first and the chapel follows as his business prospers. The film sets three founding tellings side by side (faith then prosperity; prosperity as the condition of a vow; wealth given for the building) and rules all of them undecidable under the text's own criterion, what is placed foremost. It is shot at solar noon on the day the sun stands overhead and pays off on a locked straight-down drone shot of the banyan whose shade lies exactly under it, then one vertical rise until sea and lagoon are both in the frame. The title has changed to follow the film. What to judge: first, whether a living shrine can carry a film about the aims behind offerings at all (the record's answer is that it shows no pilgrim, is shot outside both feasts, and argues that no observer can see another's aim); second, whether the church and its ground are strong enough footage without the overhead noon shot, which depends on drone permission. Corrections to the proposal and its sources are listed in the research note. Audit 2026-09-26: independent second check. Verdict KEEP WITH FIXES. Re-verified against the sources: the Tennent footnote (1850, pp. 231-232) in the Google scan, word for word; the OMI World entry; the 1999 feature; the Lanka Pradeepa page. Changed: (1) 'every account' of the founding has a tree, an image and money is false by the record's own list (the 2020 journal telling has no vow and no money); logline, two_layers and beat 1 now say 'nearly every' and name the exception; (2) the traveller telling was attributed to Bishop Bonjean in the voice and throughout, but OMI World ties only the 17th-century dating to Bonjean and gives the telling as one of 'many oral traditions'; Bonjean is removed from the voice and the attribution corrected everywhere; (3) beat 6 said Tennent 'wrote it firmly' and then set the decision factor beside him ('It does not say which this was'), which both misreports a hedged sentence ('There is reason to fear') and narrates a named person's mental factor; rewritten so the decision factor is stated as a general caution about readings, with matching changes in concept_merge, how_it_binds and the C021 link, and a new risk; (4) 'no thief would venture' is Tennent's 'it is presumed', now so in the voice; (5) beat 3 gave keeping and spending under the faith clause and added 'for their own sake', which C005-M:L9 and M:L5 do not say; now faith foremost for earning and the like, wisdom foremost for earning, keeping and spending, and M:L5 without the gloss; (6) 'The altar was this one' overclaimed a probable identification; hedged, and the 1844 mission report (one St Anne church among fourteen) added as supporting evidence; (7) the 1999 feature's merchant from the southern port at the far end of Tennent's road and its 'eighty-year-old church in 1842' (a basis for 1762) added to the disputed list; (8) 'St Joseph feast' in March changed to 'the March feast'; (9) image caption 'airliner' changed to 'aerial', which is what the file description supports; (10) the IDEA-0018 connection described a proposed rewrite as if current, now stated as conditional; a connection to IDEA-0025, which shares this film's thesis, added. Still unverified: who first recorded any founding telling; Bonjean's own text; Tennent's identification of the altar; the zenith dates for the shooting year; drone permission; whether the banyan reads as one shape from above.

suggested_location.region: Puttalam District, North Western Province: Kalpitiya Divisional Secretariat area, on the west (sea) side of the Kalpitiya peninsula, about 220 m from the Indian Ocean shore and about 3 km from the Puttalam lagoon shore to the east (verified by reverse geocoding the OSM node of the shrine to Puttalam District, and by distances to the OSM coastline). In the Catholic Diocese of Chilaw.
suggested_location.why_here: It is the one place found where a shrine's own founding tellings and the oldest printed mention of its altar both turn on the question C005 asks, what was placed in front of an act of earning, giving or guarding, and where the landscape gives a frame that can hold that question without a person in it. The tellings put faith and prosperity in different orders; the 1850 footnote describes a single band of leaves that was an offering and a guard against thieves at once. The peninsula supplies the frame: surf, a pale strip of sand, a white church and a banyan, a second, glassy water, and, twice a year at noon, a sun directly overhead that removes every shadow. District budget: Puttalam goes from 3 films to 4 (preferred), with no other GRP-02 film in the district.

historical_thread.story: The church is the pilgrimage shrine of Saint Anne on the sea side of the Kalpitiya peninsula, whose feasts draw very large crowds (the Sunday Times reported an expected 500,000 for the 2012 feast, which it called the church's 250th anniversary without saying what the count runs from). The present church's foundation was laid in 1837 by the Goan Oratorian Fr Pedro Caetano and the church completed in 1843 under Fr Pedro de Noronha (1999 feature; the 1837 foundation also in Jayasinghe 2016 as cited by Lanka Pradeepa); the Oblates took over its administration from 1850 (Fr Frédéric Mouchel), and it was enlarged in the later nineteenth century, with transepts built 1880-1884 and completed in 1887 (as cited by Lanka Pradeepa) and a bell given by the father of Fr André Mélizan (OMI World). The report of the Apostolic Vicariate of Jaffna for 1850, as quoted in the Oblates' historical dictionary, describes 'the church of St. Anne built in a handsome style and richly adorned with flowered satinwood, to which every year resort so many thousand pilgrims from every part of Ceylon and from the continent too, in order to fulfil vows'. In the same year James Emerson Tennent, who had been Colonial Secretary of Ceylon (Wikipedia gives 1846-1850), published Christianity in Ceylon (London: John Murray, 1850). In its chapter on Buddhism and demon worship (pp. 231-232) a footnote tells travellers on the road from Point de Galle to Colombo that they will notice fruit trees 'round the stem of which a band of leaves has been fastened by the owner. This is to denote that the tree has been devoted to a demon; and sometimes to Vishnu or the Kattregam dewol. Occasionally these dedications are made to the temples of Buddhu, and even to the Roman Catholic altars, as to that of St. Anne of Calpentyn. This ceremony is called Gok-bandeema, "the tying of the tender leaf," and its operation is to protect the fruit from pillage till ripe enough to be plucked and sent as an offering to the divinity to whom it has thus been consecrated. There is reason to fear, however, that on these occasions the devil is, to some extent, defrauded of his due, as the custom is, after applying a few only of the finest as an offering to the evil one, to appropriate the remainder to the use of the owner. ... so long as the wreath continues to hang upon the tree, it is presumed that no thief would venture to plunder the garden.' The shrine's beginning survives only as tradition, in several tellings. Bishop Ernest Christophe Bonjean (Vicar Apostolic of Jaffna 1868-1883, later first Archbishop of Colombo), 'according to the testimony of tradition', judged it 'most probable that the pilgrimage to this shrine began some time in the 17th century'; OMI World then gives, as one of 'many oral traditions' and without saying who recorded it, a telling in which a tired Portuguese traveller lay down under a banyan commending his soul to Saint Anne, dreamt of a small statue of the saint with two candles, woke to find it, built a small shelter, and later built a chapel as his business prospered (OMI World). The same OMI World entry quotes Bishop Caetano Antonio's report of 12 February 1844, which counts fourteen churches in the mission of Kalpity, one of them dedicated to St Anne. A 1999 newspaper feature gives two tellings: a poor Portuguese traveller who dreams of the image, finds it, and is told by the saint to build, and given gold coins to do so; and a European merchant ship dedicated to Saint Anne wrecked off the coast, the image placed in a hollow of a banyan, and the captain, a merchant from Galle, vowing to build a church if his business prospered, which he did; the same feature says the church standing in 1842 was 80 years old. A travel site citing Udugama (1983) makes the trader French and the ship a schooner named St Anne; a 2020 journal article cited by Lanka Pradeepa has a statue floated ashore from a wreck and seen giving light in a tree hollow, with no traveller and no vow.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C005 sorts the ordinary acts of earning, guarding and giving by one criterion, what is placed foremost (පෙරදැරි කර ගෙන) [C005-M:L9], against a list on which earning and guarding wealth for their own sake appear among the everyday occasions of wanting [C005-M:L5]. The shrine's tellings are three different answers to exactly that question: faith first and prosperity after (the traveller of the Oblate record), prosperity as the condition of a vow (the wrecked trader), and wealth given for the building (the gold). None of them can be ruled, because the tellings disagree about the very thing the rule needs (and one later telling has no vow and no money at all), and the film does not choose. The 1850 footnote is the documentary half: one act, a band of young leaves round a tree, which in its author's own sentence did two things, marked the fruit as an offering to the divinity and kept thieves off until it ripened. The text has a place for each aim, and none for telling them apart from outside. The author then offered a reading of the aim himself, hedged ('there is reason to fear'), of offerings made to spirits; the film sets beside it C021's account of the decision factor, which fixes on its object without separating true from false [C021-P:L45], as a caution about any reading, and never says what was in its author's mind. The concept's own question, what was in front, is therefore asked by the place's record twice, once by its legends and once by its first printed witness, and in both cases the record cannot answer it. That is what the film is about.
what_is_certain: The shrine stands at about 8.1128 N, 79.7036 E, in Puttalam District, about 220 m from the sea and about 3 km from the lagoon shore (OSM node and coastline).

Tennent's Christianity in Ceylon was published in London by John Murray in 1850; the footnote quoted is on pp. 231-232 in the chapter on demon worship, and was read in two independent scans (the 1850 Google scan and the 1998 Asian Educational Services reprint on the Internet Archive).

The footnote names 'the Roman Catholic altars, as to that of St. Anne of Calpentyn' among the recipients of dedicated trees, and describes the band of leaves as protecting the fruit from pillage until it is plucked and sent as an offering, and says that while it hangs 'it is presumed that no thief would venture to plunder the garden'.
The footnote's trees were those seen on the road between Point de Galle and Colombo; it does not describe dedicated trees on the peninsula.

The footnote's suspicion that the owner kept most of the fruit is written of offerings 'to the evil one', not of any Catholic altar, and is introduced with a hedge: 'There is reason to fear, however'.
Casie Chitty's Ceylon Gazetteer (1834) has no entry for Talawila and no mention of St Anne; its entry for Calpentyn town records 'one' Roman Catholic place of worship there, unnamed.

The 1850 report of the Apostolic Vicariate of Jaffna, as quoted by OMI World, describes the church as handsome, adorned with satinwood, and visited yearly by many thousand pilgrims from all Ceylon and the continent 'in order to fulfil vows'.
The Oblates took over the shrine's administration in 1850 (Fr Frédéric Mouchel), per OMI World.
The Sunday Times of 5 August 2012 called that year's feast the church's 250th anniversary and reported 500,000 pilgrims expected; it does not say what the count runs from.
The sun passes directly overhead at this latitude (about 8.11 N) around 11 April and around 2 September (computed from the solar declination).

OMI World ties Bishop Bonjean's record of tradition to the judgement that the pilgrimage 'most probably' began in the 17th century; it gives the traveller telling as one of 'many oral traditions' without saying who recorded it (read 2026-09-26).
OMI World quotes Bishop Caetano Antonio's report to Propaganda Fide of 12 February 1844: of fourteen churches in the mission of Kalpity, one was dedicated to St Anne.
what_is_disputed: The founding tellings, kept apart and not averaged: (1) the Oblate record's (via OMI World, given as oral tradition and not attributed to Bonjean): a Portuguese traveller, a dream of the statue with two candles, the statue found, a shelter, and a chapel built as his business prospered; (2) the 1999 feature's vision telling: a poor Portuguese traveller, the saint's instruction to build, three appearances, gold coins given; (3) the 1999 feature's shipwreck telling: a European trader's ship dedicated to St Anne, the image placed in a banyan's hollow, a vow to build a church if his business prospered, the merchant said to be from Galle; (4) the travel site's version (citing Udugama 1983): the trader French, the ship a schooner named St Anne sailing from Galle to Kalpitiya; (5) the 2020 journal version (via Lanka Pradeepa): a statue floated ashore from a wreck and gave light in a tree hollow, with no vow.

The date of the beginning: the 17th century (Bonjean, 'most probable', from tradition); the 18th century (the 1999 shipwreck telling); 1762 (implied by the 2012 '250th anniversary', whose basis the Sunday Times does not state, and by the 1999 feature's remark that the church standing in 1842 was 80 years old); 1837-1843 for the present church. Four answers, kept apart.

Whether Tennent's 'St. Anne of Calpentyn' is this shrine. Probable: it was the island's famous St Anne's shrine in 1850 and the Oblates' dictionary files it under Kalpity; but Chitty (1834) records an unnamed Roman Catholic place of worship in Calpentyn town itself (failure mode 4, a similar name). Against that, the 1844 mission report quoted by OMI World counts only one church dedicated to St Anne among the mission's fourteen, which makes the identification more likely without proving it.
Whether the banyan now in front of the church is the tree of the tellings (asserted by a travel site as 'believed to be the very same one'; no evidence).
The start of Tennent's term as Colonial Secretary (Wikipedia gives 1846; other sources are said to give 1845; not resolved, and the voice avoids the date).

The 1806 hymn: said in the Commons file description to come from a palm-leaf manuscript dated 21 March 1806 and to be printed in Bishop Edmund Peiris's St. Anne of Talavila; neither the book nor the manuscript was reached, so it stays out of the voice.
The 1943 'ship's hull' said to have surfaced a hundred years after the church's completion (1999 feature only).

what_to_film: The overhead noon on the zenith day (about 11 April or about 2 September, to be recomputed for the year and checked against an almanac): a locked drone directly above the banyan, straight down, the crown and its shade one shape; then one vertical rise, no tilt, until the church roof, the surf and the lagoon are all in frame.
Late morning of the same day: the high oblique establishing frame from over the surf, looking inland across the strip to the lagoon, locked.
The church front square-on in near-overhead light, locked, 35 mm; the façade's recesses with no shadow in them.
The banyan from the ground, 35 mm on a tripod: roots, shade, the empty ground behind; no people under it.
Coconut palms in the gardens near the church, long lens, and one trunk close from its base up, with nothing tied to any tree.
The empty feast ground and its shelters from a low tripod at noon, heat shimmer, the church small at the edge of frame.
Sound: surf on the sea side, wind in the fronds, crows; if the church bell is rung at noon on the day, record it where it falls, but do not ask for it.
suggested_location.access: On the public road along the Kalpitiya peninsula (the Etalai-Talawila road), a few hours' drive north from Colombo via Puttalam. The shrine is open daily and administered by the Catholic Diocese of Chilaw, whose permission is needed for any filming on the ground and above it. Drone flight needs Civil Aviation Authority clearance, and the peninsula has naval and air-force installations, so clearance may take time or be refused. No access, permission or drone clearance has been verified.
suggested_location.best_time: Solar noon (about 12:10 local time) on the zenith day, about 11 April or about 2 September, with the late morning for the establishing frames. Avoid the March feast and the main St Anne feast (end of July and into early August), and Holy Week in years when it falls near 11 April. April has the calmer sea; September follows the south-west monsoon winds.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research, 26 September 2026. Proposed on the blind GRP-02 selection, tested and kept with its story rebuilt. Corrections to the proposal: (1) its earliest account was the 1999 Sunday Observer feature; the altar is named in print in 1850 by Tennent, the 1850 Jaffna vicariate report is quoted by the Oblates' dictionary, a nineteenth-century record of tradition is summarised there (only the 17th-century dating is tied to Bonjean), and a hymn said to be dated 1806 is carried by a Commons file description from Bishop Edmund Peiris's book (not reached); (2) the proposal gave two founding legends, assigning the prosperity vow to the ship's captain and the gold to the traveller; the traveller telling in the Oblate record gives the prosperity to the traveller (the chapel built 'as his business prospered'), and at least five tellings exist, one with no vow at all; (3) the proposal's trader was 'Portuguese in one telling, French in another': in the sources reached the trader is 'European' (1999) or French (a travel site citing Udugama 1983), and it is the traveller who is Portuguese; (4) the 2012 '250th anniversary' is confirmed in the Sunday Times, which does not say what it counts from; 1762 is only arithmetic. Failure modes tested: 1 (Chitty's 1834 Gazetteer was downloaded and searched: no Talawila, no St Anne; the proposal did not credit it, but the searched absence is recorded, not read as denial, mode 6); 2 (the founding legends are carried only by late tellings, and Bonjean himself says 'most probable'); 3 ('500,000 pilgrims' is a newspaper expectation, used only as such); 4 ('St. Anne of Calpentyn' might be an unnamed Catholic church in the town, and searches collide with St Anne's at Talaulim in Goa); 5 (four dates for the beginning, kept apart); 7 (no 'scholars attribute' claim is used); 8 (Tennent's footnote is quoted whole, including the anti-theft purpose and the suspicion, and the suspicion's actual object, offerings to spirits, is kept). Who wrote it down: the tradition was written down by the Oblate bishop who administered the shrine's region, a party with an interest in its antiquity; the footnote was written by a Protestant colonial official in a book on the progress of Christian missions, in its chapter on demon worship. District: reverse geocoding of the OSM node returns Puttalam District; distance to coastline from OSM. Puttalam moves from 3 films to 4. Images: Commons holds one photograph of the site (the statue inside) and nothing of the church exterior, the banyan or the ground; the second image is the peninsula's landform, not the site, and is captioned so. No access, permission or drone clearance has been verified.

unknowns: No participant, access or permission has been found or confirmed; the diocese that administers the shrine has not been approached.
Whether a drone may fly directly over the shrine ground at noon (Civil Aviation Authority; nearby military installations).
Whether the banyan in front of the church still stands, how large it is, and whether its crown and shade read as one shape from directly above.
Whether the church ground is empty enough at noon on the zenith dates, which are ordinary days, not feast days.
Whether the altar named in the 1850 footnote is this shrine and not an unnamed Catholic church in the peninsula's town (see suggested_location).
The exact zenith dates for the shooting year, to be recomputed.

Who first recorded the traveller telling (OMI World does not say), Bonjean's own text, and the 1850 vicariate report were reached only through the OMI World summary; Bishop Edmund Peiris's St. Anne of Talavila was not reached.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude and awaits Chathura's review; it has not been confirmed. The Tennent footnote (1850) and the Casie Chitty entry (1834) are documentary and were read in scans of the printed texts; the Oblate record of tradition (with Bonjean's 17th-century dating) and the 1850 vicariate report are reached only through the OMI World summary; the founding tellings of 1999 and later are journalism and tradition; the zenith dates are computed; access, permissions and filming conditions are desk research and unverified. No scene or shot has been filmed.
